entries.d4b3267e13f337fdb69710d6bdfc4336157c1ad1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8873"/><div sID="gen14833" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8873"/>20. Rather, "The Lord will give"; the "though" is not in the original.<div eID="gen14833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14834" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bread of adversity--</hi>He will not deny you food enough to save you in your adversity (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.27">1Ki 22:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.127.2">Psa 127:2</reference>).<div eID="gen14834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14835" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be removed--</hi>rather, "hide themselves"; they shall no more be forced to hide themselves from persecution, but shall be openly received with reverence [Maurer]. Contrast with this <reference osisRef="Ps.74.9">Psa 74:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.8.11">Am 8:11</reference>. <div eID="gen14835" type="x-p"/>
entries.98f155a723a1a18903a0d13c87f5c466e1df960b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8874"/><div sID="gen14836" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8874"/><hi type="bold">21. word--</hi>conscience, guided by the Holy Spirit (<reference osisRef="John.16.13">Joh 16:13</reference>). <div eID="gen14836" type="x-p"/>
entries.2cefba25a774042fa348557e3714a388975c0006: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8875"/><div sID="gen14837" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8875"/><hi type="bold">22. covering of ... images--</hi>rather, "images" (formed of wood or potter's clay, and) "covered with silver." Hezekiah, and afterwards Josiah, defiled them (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.8">2Ki 23:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.14">10, 14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.1">2Ch 31:1</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.2.20">Is 2:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.7.25">De 7:25</reference>). <div eID="gen14837" type="x-p"/>
entries.3bdc37f087ecefff40e806a4cf31ae1ca7992d5e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8876"/><div sID="gen14838" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8876"/><hi type="bold">23. rain of--</hi>rather, "for thy seed." Physical prosperity accompanies national piety; especially under the Old Testament. The early rain fell soon after the seed was sown in October or November; the latter rain in the spring, before the ripening of the corn. Both were needed for a good harvest.<div eID="gen14838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14839" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">increase--</hi>the produce.<div eID="gen14839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14840" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fat--</hi>bread made of the best wheat flour (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.49.20">Ge 49:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.14">De 32:14</reference>). <div eID="gen14840" type="x-p"/>
entries.2df20d770c96657a0d3870ad97414d6ee8605dc1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8877"/><div sID="gen14841" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8877"/><hi type="bold">24. ear--</hi>that is, till. Asses were employed in tillage, as well as oxen (<reference osisRef="Deut.22.10">De 22:10</reference>).<div eID="gen14841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14842" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">clean--</hi>rather, salted provender [Gesenius]. The Arab proverb is, "Sweet provender is as bread to camels--salted provender as confectionery." The very cattle shall share the coming felicity. Or else, well-fermented maslin, that is, provender formed of a mixture of various substances: grain, beans, vetches, hay, and salt.<div eID="gen14842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14843" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">winnowed--</hi>not as it is usually given to cattle before it is separated from the chaff; the grain shall be so abundant that it shall be given winnowed.<div eID="gen14843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14844" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shovel--</hi>by which the grain was thrown up in the wind to separate it from the chaff.<div eID="gen14844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14845" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fan--</hi>an instrument for winnowing. <div eID="gen14845" type="x-p"/>
entries.1ce0f2dfb612895f59e880deb7a87fb1cc6956a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8878"/><div sID="gen14846" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8878"/>25. Even the otherwise barren hills shall then be well-watered (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.3">Is 44:3</reference>).<div eID="gen14846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14847" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the day, &c.--</hi>when the disobedient among the Jews shall have been slain, as foretold in <reference osisRef="Isa.30.16">Is 30:16</reference>: "towers," that is, mighty men (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.15">Is 2:15</reference>). Or else, the towers of the Assyrian Sennacherib, or of Babylon, types of all enemies of God's people. <div eID="gen14847" type="x-p"/>
entries.488d60c80b47240701438f286d5d5b33e2fe0d4b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8879"/><div sID="gen14848" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8879"/>26. Image from the heavenly bodies to express the increase of spiritual light and felicity. "Sevenfold" implies the perfection of that felicity, seven being the sacred number. It shall also be literally fulfilled hereafter in the heavenly city (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.19">Is 60:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.60.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.23">Re 21:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.24">24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.5">22:5</reference>).<div eID="gen14848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14849" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">breach--</hi>the wound, or calamity, sent by God on account of their sins (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.5">Is 1:5</reference>). <div eID="gen14849" type="x-p"/>
entries.b24be8945cf0619c8001a574189bc2bc9f6843a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8880"/><div sID="gen14850" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8880"/><hi type="bold">27. name of ... Lord--</hi>that is, Jehovah Himself (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.5">Psa 44:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.54.1">54:1</reference>); represented as a storm approaching and ready to burst over the Assyrians (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.30">Is 30:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.31">31</reference>).<div eID="gen14850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14851" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">burden ... is heavy--</hi>literally, "grievousness is the flame," that is, the flame which darts from Him is grievous. Or else (as the Hebrew means an "uplifting") the uprising cloud is grievous [G. V. Smith]; the gathering cloud gradually rising till it bursts. <div eID="gen14851" type="x-p"/>
entries.015a41bf0df5fe9a7c064f129c1d31e306230540: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8881"/><div sID="gen14852" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8881"/>28. (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">Is 11:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.8">2Th 2:8</reference>).<div eID="gen14852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14853" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reach ... neck--</hi>the most extreme danger; yet as the head, or capital of Judah, was to be spared (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.8">Is 8:8</reference>), so the head, or sovereign of Assyria, Sennacherib, should escape.<div eID="gen14853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14854" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sieve of vanity--</hi>Rather, "the winnowing fan of destruction" [Lowth] (<reference osisRef="Isa.41.16">Is 41:16</reference>).<div eID="gen14854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14855" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bridle in ... jaws--</hi>as prisoners are represented in the Assyrian inscriptions (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.29">Is 37:29</reference>).<div eID="gen14855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14856" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">causing ... to err--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.63.17">Is 63:17</reference>). "People," Hebrew, "peoples," namely, the various races composing the Assyrian armies (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.26">Is 5:26</reference>). <div eID="gen14856" type="x-p"/>
entries.7312a1c4ee3f126f4f8b66868faf1fbe4ec5c1ce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8882"/><div sID="gen14857" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8882"/><hi type="bold">29. the night ... solemnity--</hi>As in the passover night ye celebrate your deliverance from Egypt, so shall ye celebrate your rescue from Assyrian bondage. Translate, "the solemnity" (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.42">Ex 12:42</reference>).<div eID="gen14857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14858" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">goeth with a pipe--</hi>or flute. They used to go up to Jerusalem ("the mountain of the Lord," Zion) at the three feasts with music and gladness (<reference osisRef="Deut.16.16">De 16:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezra.2.65">Ezr 2:65</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.122.1-Ps.122.4">Psa 122:1-4</reference>). <div eID="gen14858" type="x-p"/>
entries.2ea79657410f01c616d5336a13d65d8001560898: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8883"/><div sID="gen14859" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8883"/>30. Jehovah's "glorious voice," raised against the enemy (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.27">Is 30:27</reference>), is again mentioned here, in contrast to the music (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.29">Is 30:29</reference>) with which His people shall come to worship Him.<div eID="gen14859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14860" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lighting down of ... arm--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.30.32">Is 30:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.38.2">Psa 38:2</reference>). The descent of His arm in striking.<div eID="gen14860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14861" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">scattering--</hi>namely, a blast that scatters, or an "inundation" [Maurer]. <div eID="gen14861" type="x-p"/>
entries.a098a3c7672553aa5bc9ef0c7b0db7d3ecf31126: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8884"/><div sID="gen14862" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8884"/>31. The Assyrian rod which beat shall itself be beaten, and that by the mere voice of the Lord, that is, an unseen divine agency (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.5">Is 10:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.24">24</reference>). <div eID="gen14862" type="x-p"/>
entries.f86a70f5c913b8599bf53ee08c0047a9bb833d3f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8885"/><div sID="gen14863" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8885"/><hi type="bold">32. grounded--</hi>rather, "decreed," "appointed" [Maurer].<div eID="gen14863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14864" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">staff--</hi>the avenging rod.<div eID="gen14864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14865" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">him--</hi>the Assyrian; type of all God's enemies in every age. Margin and Maurer construe, "Every passing through (infliction, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.15">Is 28:15</reference>) of the appointed rod, which, &c., shall be with tabrets," that is, accompanied with joy on the part of the rescued peoples.<div eID="gen14865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14866" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">battles of shaking--</hi>that is, shock of battles (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.16">Is 19:16</reference>; compare "sift ... sieve," <reference osisRef="Isa.30.28">Is 30:28</reference>).<div eID="gen14866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14867" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with it--</hi>namely, Assyria. <div eID="gen14867" type="x-p"/>
entries.e436600b70822097b6fdbcd0832ca1ff4db626a4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8886"/><div sID="gen14868" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8886"/><hi type="bold">33. Tophet--</hi>literally, "A place of abomination"; the valley of the sons of Hinnom, southeast of Jerusalem, where Israel offered human sacrifices to Moloch by fire; hence a place of burning (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.10">2Ki 23:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.31">Jr 7:31</reference>). Latterly Gehinnom or Gehenna, that is, valley of Hinnom, was the receptacle of the refuse of the city, to consume which fires were constantly burning. Hence it came to express hell, the place of torment. In the former sense it was a fit place to symbolize the funeral pyre of the Assyrian army (not that it actually perished there); the Hebrews did not burn, but buried their dead, but the heathen Assyrians are to be burnt as a mark of ignominy. In the latter sense Tophet is the receptacle "prepared for the devil (antitype to the king, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.12-Isa.14.15">Is 14:12-15</reference>) and his angels," and unbelieving men (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.22">Mt 5:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.41">25:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.9.43">Mr 9:43</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.9.44">44</reference>). <chapter eID="Isa.30"/>

entries.5fc40555f9b9a381633f2be41a5f236b5a68f512: <div eID="gen27722" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen27723" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27724" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27724" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27723" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27725" type="x-p"/> The Jews reproved for their reliance on Egypt, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.1-Isa.30.7">Isa 30:1-7</reference>. Threatened for their obstinate adherence to this alliance, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.8-Isa.30.17">Isa 30:8-17</reference>. Images the most elegant and lofty, by which the intense gloriousness of Messiah's reign at the period when all Israel shall be added to the Church is beautifully set forth, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.18-Isa.30.26">Isa 30:18-26</reference>. Dreadful fall of Sennacherib's army, an event most manifestly typical of the terrible and sudden overthrow of Antichrist; as, unless this typical reference be admitted, no possible connection can be imagined between the stupendous events which took place in Hezekiah's reign, and the very remote and inconceivably more glorious displays of Divine vengeance and mercy in the days of the Messiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.27-Isa.30.33">Isa 30:27-33</reference>. <div eID="gen27725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27726" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen27726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27727" type="x-p"/> And that cover with a covering "Who ratify covenants" - Hebrews "Who pour out a libation." Sacrifice and libation were ceremonies constantly used, in ancient times by most nations in the ratifying of covenants: a libation therefore is used for a covenant, as in Greek the word σπονδη, for the same reason, stands for both. This seems to be the most easy explication of the Hebrew phrase, and it has the authority of the Septuagint, εποιησατε συνθηκας.
entries.2361d1fd55a2ce79003aee1f7cad1cf139dd8644: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen27727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27728" type="x-p"/> Hanes - Six MSS. of Kennicott's, and perhaps six others, with four of De Rossi's, read חנם chinnam, in vain, for הנס Hanes; and so also the Septuagint, who read likewise יגעו yageu, labored, for יגיעו yaggiu, arrived at.
entries.bfdc36c2c800630893a53306ff69ab2b7ee3e9ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen27728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27729" type="x-p"/> Were - ashamed - Eight MSS. (one ancient) of Kennicott's, and ten of De Rossi's, read הביש hobish, without א aleph. So the Chaldee and Vulgate. <div eID="gen27729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27730" type="x-p"/> But a shame "But proved even a shame" - Four MSS. (three ancient) after כי ki, add אם im, unless, which seems wanted to complete the phrase in its usual form.
entries.bf105efc8fbfe3c1744b16a10178e0a1c7814261: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen27730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27731" type="x-p"/> The burden - משא massa seems here to be taken in its proper sense; the load, not the oracle. The same subject is continued; and there seems to be no place here for a new title to a distinct prophecy. <div eID="gen27731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27732" type="x-p"/> Does not burden of the beasts of the South in this place relate to the presents sent by Hoshea king of Israel to the South - to Egypt, which lay south of Judea, to engage the Egyptians to succor him against the king of Assyria? <div eID="gen27732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27733" type="x-p"/> Into the land of trouble and anguish "Through a land of distress and difficulty" - The same deserts are here spoken of which the Israelites passed through when they came out of Egypt, which Moses describes, <reference osisRef="Deu.8.15">Deu 8:15</reference>, as "that great and terrible wilderness wherein were fiery serpents, and scorpions, and drought; where there was no water. "And which was designed to be a kind of barrier between them and Egypt, of which the Lord had said, "Ye shall henceforth return no more that way," <reference osisRef="Deu.17.16">Deu 17:16</reference>. <div eID="gen27733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27734" type="x-p"/> Shall not profit them - A MS. adds in the margin the word למו lamo, them, which seems to have been lost out of the text: it is authorized by the Septuagint and Vulgate.
entries.92b4e30a4eb33c6352397111d5870d4efe3589a1: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen27734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27735" type="x-p"/> Their strength is to sit still "Rahab the Inactive" - The two last words, הם שבת hem shabeth, joined into one, make the participle pihel המשבת hammeshabbeth. I find the learned Professor Doederlein, in his version of Isaiah, and note on this place, has given the same conjecture; which he speaks of as having been formerly published by him. A concurrence of different persons in the same conjecture adds to it a greater degree of probability.
entries.0d3371df002516b91481744d38f8ee59df05fa3d: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen27735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27736" type="x-p"/> For ever and ever "For a testimony for ever" - לעד leed. So the Syriac, Chaldee, Vulgate, and Septuagint, in MSS. Pachom. and 1. D. 2: εις μαρτυριον, which two words have been lost out of the other copies of the Septuagint.
entries.70d61cd00e6ffb4fd33a2bc7f4406beae983ed40: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen27736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27737" type="x-p"/> In oppression "In obliquity" - בעקש beakesh, transposing the two last letters of בעשק beoshek, in oppression, which seems not to belong to this place: a very probable conjecture of Houbigant.
entries.5350c9c4c712a6a4bbe3ba13f7d7108abebdb346: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen27737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27738" type="x-p"/> Swelling out to a high wall "A swelling in a high wall" - It has been observed before, that the buildings of Asia generally consist of little better than what we call mud walls. "All the houses at Ispahan, "says Thevenot, Vol. II., p. 159, "are built of bricks made of clay and straw, and dried in the sun; and covered with a plaster made of a fine white stone. In other places in Persia the houses are built with nothing else but such bricks, made with tempered clay and chopped straw, well mingled together, and dried in the sun, and then used: but the least rain dissolves them. "Sir John Chardin's MS. remark on this place of Isaiah is very apposite: Murs en Asie etant faits de terre se fendent ainsi par milieu et de haut en bas. "The walls in Asia being made of earth often cleave from top to bottom." This shouts clearly how obvious and expressive the image is. The psalmist has in the same manner made use of it, to express sudden and utter destruction: - "Ye shall be slain all of you; <div eID="gen27738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27739" type="x-p"/> Ye shall be like an inclining wall, like a shattered fence." <reference osisRef="Psa.62.4">Psa 62:4</reference>.
entries.425667a06042d364bb40e8c43ed84b4499844a4d: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen27739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27740" type="x-p"/> He shall not spare "And spareth it not" - Five MSS. add the conjunction ו vau to the negative; ולא velo.
entries.9ef7a5b6735de4fb5d71065ed8a6579d2cad423b: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen27740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27741" type="x-p"/> At the rebuke of five shall ye flee "At the rebuke of five, ten thousand of you shall flee" - In the second line of this verse a word is manifestly omitted, which should answer to one thousand in the first: the Septuagint supply πολλοι, רבים rabbim. But the true word is רבבה rebabah, as I am persuaded any one will be convinced, who will compare the following passages with this place: - "How should one chase a thousand; <div eID="gen27741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27742" type="x-p"/> And two put ten thousand (רבבה) to flight?" <reference osisRef="Deu.32.30">Deu 32:30</reference>. "And five of you shall chase a hundred; <div eID="gen27742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27743" type="x-p"/> And a hundred of you shall chase (רבבה) ten thousand." <reference osisRef="Lev.26.8">Lev 26:8</reference>.
entries.4ccbf691d621977c150feca9b58c648ccc257d10: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen27743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27744" type="x-p"/> And therefore will he be exalted "Even for this shall he expect in silence" - For ירום yarum, he shall be exalted, which belongs not to this place, Houbigant reads ידום yadum, he shall be silent: and so it seems to be in a MS. Another MS. instead of it reads ישוב yashub, he shall return. The mistakes occasioned by the similitude of the letters ד daleth and ר resh are very frequent, as the reader may have already observed.
entries.2f2b8f235c0acbb9bdfd21c34b66bb72d4a66464: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen27744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27745" type="x-p"/> For the people shall dwell in Zion "When a holy people shall dwell in Sion" - Λαος ἁγιος, Septuagint; עם קדוש am kadosh. The word קדוש dro kadosh, lost out of the text, but happily supplied by the Septuagint, clears up the sense, otherwise extremely obscure. When the rest of the cities of the land were taken by the king of Assyria, Zion was preserved, and all that were in it. <div eID="gen27745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27746" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt weep no more "Thou shalt implore him with weeping" - The negative particle לא lo is not acknowledged by the Septuagint. It may perhaps have been written by mistake for לו lo, to him, of which there are many examples.
entries.104af0822cce372e367579fa9edcbae0a1e695e7: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen27746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27747" type="x-p"/> Though the Lord "Though Jehovah" - For אדני Adonai, sixteen MSS. and three editions have יהוה Yehovah, many of De Rossi's have the same reading; all my own have יהוה Yehovah.
entries.59311e45248387432584b0afd4469f45a44b040f: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen27747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27748" type="x-p"/> When ye turn to the right hand, and when ye turn to the left "Turn not aside, to the right or to the left" - The Syriac Chaldee, and Vulgate, translate as if, instead of כי־וכי ki-vechi, they read לא־ולא lo-velo.
entries.45553de6f159039a18267dcfb1fec4ec2374a2d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen27748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27749" type="x-p"/> Ye shall defile "Ye shall treat as defiled" - The very prohibition of Moses, <reference osisRef="Deu.7.25">Deu 7:25</reference>, only thrown out of the prose into the poetical form: "The graven images of their gods ye shall burn with fire: thou shalt not desire the silver or the gold that is on them; nor take it unto thee, lest thou be snared therein; for it is an abomination to Jehovah thy God."
entries.9c9a865a9face338fe4d60112d162899998a79c3: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen27749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27750" type="x-p"/> When the towers fall "When the mighty fall" - מגדלים migdalim, μεγαλους, Sym.; μεγαλυνομενους, Aquila; רברבין rabrebin, Chard.; all signifying mighty sizes.
entries.6988d520032e67337ae26cdb2eced9271cf0d34f: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen27750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27751" type="x-p"/> Shall be sevenfold - The text adds כאור שבעת הימים keor shibath haiyamayim, "as the light of seven days, "a manifest gloss, taken in from the margin; it is not in most of the copies of the Septuagint. It interrupts the rhythmical construction, and obscures the sense by a false, or at least an unnecessary, interpretation. <div eID="gen27751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27752" type="x-p"/> By moon, sun, light, are to be understood the abundance of spiritual and temporal felicity with which God should bless them in the days of the Messiah, which should be sevenfold, i.e. vastly exceed all that they had ever before possessed.
entries.346f34a52c64efb798631a2a9e79868e58291571: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen27752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27753" type="x-p"/> And the burden thereof is heavy "And the flame raged violently" - משאה massaah; this word seems to be rightly rendered in our translation, the flame, <reference osisRef="Jdg.20.38">Jdg 20:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jdg.20.40">Jdg 20:40</reference>, etc.; a sign of fire, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.1">Jer 6:1</reference>; called properly משאת masseeth, an elevation, from its tending upwards.
entries.c31c6234fc1531ed952f70412d4f74d2be4e2e10: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen27753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27754" type="x-p"/> To sift the nations with a sieve of vanity "To toss the nations with the van of perdition" - The word להנפה lahanaphah is in its form very irregular. Kimchi says it is for להניף lehaniph. Houbigant supposes it to be a mistake, and shows the cause of it; the joining it to the ה he, which should begin the following word. The true reading is להניף הגוים lehaniph haggoyim, "to sift the nations." <div eID="gen27754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27755" type="x-p"/> The Vulgate seems to be the only one of the ancient interpreters who has explained rightly the sense; but he has dropped the image: ad perdendas gentes in nihilum, "to reduce the nations to nothing. "Kimchi's explanation is to the following effect:" נפה naphah is a van with which they winnow corn; and its use is to cleanse the corn from the chaff and straw: but the van with which God will winnow the nations will be the van of emptiness or perdition; for nothing useful shall remain behind, but all shall come to nothing, and perish. In like manner, a bridle is designed to guide the horse in the right way; but the bridle which God will put in the jaws of the people shall not direct them aright, but shall make them err, and lead them into destruction." This latter image the prophet has applied to the same subject afterwards, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.29">Isa 37:29</reference> : - "I will put my bridle in thy jaws, And turn thee back by the way in which thou camest." <div eID="gen27755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27756" type="x-p"/> And as for the former it is to be observed, that the van of the ancients was a large instrument, somewhat like a shovel, with a long handle, with which they tossed the corn mixed with the chaff and chopped straw into the air, that the wind might separate them. See Hammond on <reference osisRef="Mat.3.12">Mat 3:12</reference>. <div eID="gen27756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27757" type="x-p"/> There shall be a bridle in the jaws - A metaphor taken from a headstrong, unruly horse: the bridle checks, restrains, and directs him. <div eID="gen27757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27758" type="x-p"/> What the true God does in restraining sinners has been also attributed to the false gods of the heathen. Thus Aeschylus, prom. Vinct. 691: - αλλ' επηναγκαζε νιν Διος χαλινος προς βιαν πρασσειν ταδε. "But the bridle of Jupiter violently constrained him to do these things."
entries.11f80fbb9b30c9853e2614f65bd5fa66a4bb6849: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen27758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27759" type="x-p"/> The Lord shall cause his glorious voice to be heard - Kimchi understands this of the great destruction of the Assyrian host by the angel of the Lord. Instead of בזעף אץ bezaaph ats, "with swift anger, "five of Dr. Kennicott's MSS. and one of my own, read בזעם אף bezaam aph, "with detestation indignant." For אץ ats, "swift, "which is the common reading, forty-two of Kennicott's, forty-three of De Rossi's, and two of my own, have אץ ats, "wrath or fury." The former reading, אץ ats, is not found in any Bible previously to that of Van der Hooght, in 1705; and there it seems to be a typographical mistake.
entries.ad9769c6616282ecc0cff272d3a281ed06f2ef8d: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen27759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27760" type="x-p"/> Which smote with a rod "He that was ready to smite with his staff" - "Post אשור ashshur, forte excidit אשר asher." - Secker. After אשור ashshur, probably אשר asher, "which, "has been omitted.
entries.f70c4085d41b1626d6c7fa85150c5511b4574025: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen27760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27761" type="x-p"/> The grounded staff "The rod of his correction" - For מוסדה musadah, the grounded staff, of which no one yet has been able to make any tolerable sense, Le Clerc conjectured מוסרה musarah, of correction; (see <reference osisRef="Pro.22.15">Pro 22:15</reference>); and so it is in two MSS., (one of them ancient), and seems to be so in the Bodleian MS. The Syriac has דשוע בדה deshuebedah, Virgo domans, vet subjectionis, "the taming rod, or rod of subjection." <div eID="gen27761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27762" type="x-p"/> With tabrets and harps - With every demonstration of joy and thanksgiving for the destruction of the enemy in so wonderful a manner: with hymns of praise, accompanied with musical instruments. See <reference osisRef="Isa.30.29">Isa 30:29</reference>. <div eID="gen27762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27763" type="x-p"/> With it "Against them" - For בה bah. against her, fifty-two MSS. and five editions read בם bam, against them.
entries.daac9eaf05dd2293ccdcdea9024563f287050f37: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen27763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27764" type="x-p"/> For Tophet is ordained - Tophet is a valley very near to Jerusalem, to the southeast, called also the valley of Hinnom or Gehenna; where the Canaanites, and afterwards the Israelites, sacrificed their children, by making them pass through the fire, that is, by burning them in the fire, to Molech, as some suppose. It is therefore used for a place of punishment by fire; and by our blessed Savior in the Gospel for hell-fire, as the Jews themselves had applied it. See Chald. on <reference osisRef="Isa.33.14">Isa 33:14</reference>, where מוקדי עלם mokedey olam is rendered "the Gehenna of everlasting fire." Here the place where the Assyrian army was destroyed is called Tophet by a metonymy; for the Assyrian army was destroyed probably at a greater distance from Jerusalem, and quite on the opposite side of it: for Nob is mentioned as the last station, from which the king of Assyria should threaten Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.32">Isa 10:32</reference>, where the prophet seems to have given a very exact chorographical description of his march in order to attack the city; which however he never reached. - L.  <chapter eID="Isa.30"/> <div eID="gen27764" type="x-p"/>

entries.ce8cc4f5270650088cafed052297ae7568bedfe0: <reference osisRef="Isa.30.1-Isa.30.5">Isa 30:1-5</reference> <div eID="gen13186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13187" type="x-p"/> The plan which, according to <reference osisRef="Isa.29.15">Isa 29:15</reference>, was already projected and prepared in the deepest secrecy, is now much further advanced. The negotiations by means of ambassadors have already been commenced; but the prophet condemns what he can no longer prevent. <hi type="italic">“Woe to the stubborn children, saith Jehovah, to drive plans, and not by my impulse, and to plait alliance, and not according to my Spirit, to heap sin upon sin: that go away to travel down to Egypt, without having asked my mouth, to fly to Pharaoh’s shelter, and to conceal themselves under the shadow of Egypt. And Pharaoh’s shelter becomes a shame to them, and the concealment under the shadow of Egypt a disgrace. For Judah’s princes have appeared in Zoan, and his ambassadors arrive in Hanes. They will all have to be ashamed of a people useless to them, that brings no help and no use, but shame, and also reproach.”</hi> <hi type="italic">Sōrerı̄m</hi> is followed by infinitives with <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.5.22">Isa 5:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.3.8">Isa 3:8</reference>): who are bent upon it in their obstinacy. <hi type="italic">Massēkhâh</hi> designates the alliance as a plait (<hi type="italic">massēkheth</hi>). According to Cappellus and others, it designates it as formed with a libation (σπονδη, from σπένδεσθαι); but the former is certainly the more correct view, inasmuch as <hi type="italic">massēkhâh</hi> (from <hi type="italic">nâsakh</hi>, <hi type="italic">fundere</hi>) signifies a cast, and hence it is more natural here to take <hi type="italic">nâsakh</hi> as equivalent to <hi type="italic">sâkhakh</hi>, <hi type="italic">plectere</hi> (Jerome: <hi type="italic">ordiremini telam</hi>). The context leaves no doubt as to the meaning of the adverbial expressions ולא־מנּי and ולא־רוּחי, viz., without its having proceeded from me, and without my Spirit being there. “Sin upon sin:” inasmuch as they carry out further and further to perfect realization the thought which was already a sinful one in itself. The prophet now follows for himself the ambassadors, who are already on the road to the country of the Nile valley. He sees them arrive in Zoan, and watches them as they proceed thence into Hanes. He foresees and foretells what a disgraceful opening of their eyes will attend the reward of this untheocratical beginning. On <hi type="italic">lâ‛ōz b'</hi>, see at <reference osisRef="Isa.10.31">Isa 10:31</reference> : <hi type="italic">‛ōz</hi> is the infinitive constr. of <hi type="italic">‛ūz</hi>; <hi type="italic">mâ‛ōz</hi>, on the contrary, is a derivative of <hi type="italic">‛âzaz</hi>, to be strong. The suffixes of שׂריו (his princes) and מלאכיו (his ambassadors) are supposed by Hitzig, Ewald, and Knobel, who take a different view of what is said, to refer to the princes and ambassadors of Pharaoh. But this is by no means warranted on the ground that the prophet cannot so immediately transfer to Zoan and Hanes the ambassadors of Judah, who were still on their journey according to Isa 30:2. The prophet’s vision overleaps the existing stage of the desire for this alliance; he sees the great men of his nation already suing for the favour of Egypt, first of all in Zoan, and then still further in Hanes, and at once foretells the shameful termination of this self-desecration of the people of Jehovah. The lxx give for יגיעוּ חנּס, μάτην κοπιάσουσιν, i.e., ייגעוּ סהנּם, and Knobel approves this reading; but it is a misunderstanding, which only happens to have fallen out a little better this time than the rendering ὡς Δαυίδ given for כּדּוּר in Isa 29:3. If <hi type="italic">chinnâm</hi> had been the original reading, it would hardly have entered any one’s mind to change it into <hi type="italic">chânēs</hi>. The latter was the name of a city on an island of the Nile in Central Egypt, the later Heracleopolis (Eg. <hi type="italic">Hnēs</hi>; <hi type="italic">Ehnēs</hi>), the <hi type="italic">Anysis</hi> of Herodotus (ii. 137). On <hi type="italic">Zoan</hi>, see at Isa 19:11. At that time the Tanitic dynasty was reigning, the dynasty preceding the Ethiopian. Tanis and Anysis were the two capitals. הבאישׁ (= היבשׁ =( ה, a metaplastic <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi> of יבשׁ = בּושׁ, a different word from יבשׁ) is incorrectly pointed for הבאישׁ, like ריאשׁנה (<hi type="italic">keri</hi>) for ראישׁנה in Jos 21:10. הבאישׁ signifies elsewhere, “to make stinking” (to calumniate, <reference osisRef="Prov.13.5">Pro 13:5</reference>), or “to come into ill odour” (<reference osisRef="1Sam.27.12">1Sa 27:12</reference>); here, however, it means to be put to shame (בּאשׁ = בּושׁ).
entries.1a032748f3522d750b7062cef84f5e8f4e6edc2d: <reference osisRef="Isa.30.6-Isa.30.7">Isa 30:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen13187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13188" type="x-p"/> The prophet’s address is hardly commenced, however, when a heading is introduced of the very same kind as we have already met with several times in the cycle of prophecies against the heathen nations. Gesenius, Hitzig, Umbreit, and Knobel, rid themselves of it by pronouncing it a gloss founded upon a misunderstanding. But nothing is more genuine in the whole book of Isaiah than the words <hi type="italic">massâ' bahămōth negebh</hi> . The heading is emblematical, like the four headings in chapters 21, 22. And the <hi type="italic">massâ'</hi> embraces <reference osisRef="Isa.30.6">Isa 30:6</reference>, Isa 30:7. Then follows the command to write it on a table by itself. The heading is an integral part of the smaller whole. Isaiah breaks off his address to communicate an oracle relating to the Egyptian treaty, which Jehovah has specially commanded him to hand down to posterity. The same interruption would take place if we expunged the heading; for in any case it was <reference osisRef="Isa.30.6">Isa 30:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.7">Isa 30:7</reference> that he was to write upon a table. This is not an address to the people, but the preliminary text, the application of which is determined afterwards. The prophet communicates in the form of a citation what has been revealed to him by God, and then states what God has commanded him to do with it. We therefore enclose <reference osisRef="Isa.30.6">Isa 30:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.7">Isa 30:7</reference> in inverted commas as a quotation, and render the short passage, which is written in the tone of chapter 21, as follows: <hi type="italic">“Oracle concerning the water-oxen of the south: Through a land of distress and confinement, whence the lioness and lion, adders and flying dragons; they carry their possessions on the shoulders of asses’ foals, and their treasures on the humps of camels, to a nation that profits nothing. And Egypt, worthlessly and hollowly will they help; therefore I call this Egypt, Great-mouth that sits still.”</hi> The “water-ox of the south” is the Nile-horse; and this is the emblem of Egypt, the land of the south (in Daniel and Zechariah Babylonia is “the land of the north”). <hi type="italic">Bahămōth</hi> is the construct of <hi type="italic">behēmōth</hi> (Job 40), which is a Hebraized from of an Egyptian word, <hi type="italic">p</hi>-<hi type="italic">ehe</hi>-<hi type="italic">mau</hi> (though the word itself has not yet been met with), i.e., the ox of the water, or possibly <hi type="italic">p</hi>-<hi type="italic">ehe</hi>-<hi type="italic">mau</hi>-<hi type="italic">t</hi> (with the feminine article at the close, though in <hi type="italic">hesmut</hi>, another name for a female animal, <hi type="italic">mut</hi> = <hi type="italic">t . mau</hi> signifies “the mother:” see at <reference osisRef="Job.40.15">Job 40:15</reference>). The animal referred to is the hippopotamus, which is called <hi type="italic">bomarino</hi> in Italian, Arab. the Nile-horse or water-pig. The emblem of Egypt in other passages of the Old Testament is <hi type="italic">tannin</hi>, the water-snake, or <hi type="italic">leviathan</hi>, the crocodile. In <reference osisRef="Ps.78.31">Psa 78:31</reference> this is called <hi type="italic">chayyath qâneh</hi>, “the beast of the reed,” though Hengstenberg supposes that the Nile-horse is intended there. This cannot be maintained, however; but in the passage before us this emblem is chosen, just because the fat, swine-like, fleshy colossus, whose belly nearly touches the ground as it walks, is a fitting image of Egypt, a land so boastful and so eager to make itself thick and broad, and yet so slow to exert itself in the interest of others, and so unwilling to move from the spot. This is also implied in the name <hi type="italic">rahabh</hi>-<hi type="italic">hēm</hi>-<hi type="italic">shâb</hi>. <hi type="italic">Rahab</hi> is a name applied to Egypt in other passages also (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.9">Isa 51:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.87.4">Psa 87:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.11">Psa 89:11</reference>), and that in the senses attested by the lxx at <reference osisRef="Job.26.12">Job 26:12</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.9.13">Isa 9:13</reference>), viz., κῆτος, a sea-monster, <hi type="italic">monstrum marinum</hi>. Here the name has the meaning common in other passages, viz., violence, domineering pride, boasting (ἀλαζονεία, as one translator renders it). הם is a term of comparison, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.14.2-Gen.14.3">Gen 14:2-3</reference>, etc.; the plural refers to the people called rahabh. Hence the meaning is either, “The bragging people, they are sit-still;” or, “Boast-house, they are idlers.” To this deceitful land the ambassadors of Judah were going with rich resources (<hi type="italic">chăyâlı̄m</hi>, <hi type="italic">opes</hi>) on the shoulder of asses’ foals, and on the hump (<hi type="italic">dabbesheth</hi>, from <hi type="italic">dâbhash</hi>, according to Luzzatto related to <hi type="italic">gâbhash</hi>, to be hilly) of camels, without shrinking from the difficulties and dangers of the road through the desert, where lions and snakes spring out now here and now there (מהם, neuter, as in Zep 2:7, comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.38.16">Isa 38:16</reference>; see also <reference osisRef="Deut.8.15">Deu 8:15</reference>; Num 21:6). Through this very desert, through which God had led their fathers when He redeemed them out of the bondage of Egypt, they were now marching to purchase the friendship of Egypt, though really, whatever might be the pretext which they offered, it was only to deceive themselves; for the vainglorious land would never keep the promises that it made.
entries.f779356add0aa99dc69333cf4fc75af05c00dc6a: <reference osisRef="Isa.30.8">Isa 30:8</reference> <div eID="gen13188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13189" type="x-p"/> So runs the divine oracle to which the following command refers. <hi type="italic">“Now go, write it on a table with them, and note it in a book, and let it stand there fore future days, for ever, to eternity.”</hi> The suffixes of <hi type="italic">kothbâh</hi> (write it) and <hi type="italic">chuqqâh</hi> (note it) refer in a neuter sense to <reference osisRef="Isa.30.6">Isa 30:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.7">Isa 30:7</reference>; and the expression “go” is simply a general summons to proceed to the matter (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.22.15">Isa 22:15</reference>). <hi type="italic">Sēpher</hi> could be used interchangeably with <hi type="italic">lūăch</hi>, because a single leaf, the contents of which were concluded, was called <hi type="italic">sēpher</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.17.14">Exo 17:14</reference>). Isaiah was to write the oracle upon a table, a separate leaf of durable material; and that “with them,” i.e., so that his countrymen might have it before their eyes (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.8.1">Isa 8:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.2">Hab 2:2</reference>). It was to be a memorial for posterity. The reading לעד (Sept., Targ., Syr.) for לעד is appropriate, though quite unnecessary. The three indications of time form a climax: for futurity, for the most remote future, for the future without end.
entries.9336b58db31bae64415b51785b551ad62f79986d: <reference osisRef="Isa.30.9-Isa.30.11">Isa 30:9-11</reference> <div eID="gen13189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13190" type="x-p"/> It was necessary that the worthlessness of the help of Egypt should be placed in this way before the eyes of the people. <hi type="italic">“For it is a refractory people, lying children, children who do not like to hear the instruction of Jehovah, who say to the seers, See not; and to the prophets, Prophesy not unto us right things! Speak flatteries to us! Get out of the way, turn aside from the path, remove from our face the Holy One of Israel.”</hi> On the expression <hi type="italic">‛am merı̄</hi> (a people of stubbornness), see at Isa 3:8. The vowel-pointing of כחשׁהים follows the same rule as that of החכם. The prophet traces back their words to an unvarnished expression of their true meaning, just as he does in Isa 28:15. They forbid the prophets of Jehovah to prophesy, more especially <hi type="italic">nekhōchōth</hi>, straight or true things (things not agreeable to their own wishes), but would rather hear <hi type="italic">chălâqōth</hi>, i.e., smooth, insinuating, and flattering things, and even <hi type="italic">mahăthallōth</hi> (from <hi type="italic">hâthal</hi>, Talm. <hi type="italic">tal</hi>, <hi type="italic">ludere</hi>), i.e., illusions or deceits. Their desire was to be entertained and lauded, not repelled and instructed. The prophets are to adopt another course (מנּי only occurs here, and that twice, instead of the more usual מנּי = מן, after the form אלי, עלי), and not trouble them any more with the Holy One of Israel, whom they (at least Isaiah, who is most fond of calling Jehovah by this name) have always in their mouths.
entries.f7bb6c5d6e495a7a7b1560ddbab75744158f5716: <reference osisRef="Isa.30.12-Isa.30.14">Isa 30:12-14</reference> <div eID="gen13190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13191" type="x-p"/> Thus do they fall out with Jehovah and the bearers of His word. <hi type="italic">“Therefore thus saith the Holy One of Israel, Because ye dislike this word, and put your trust in force and shufflings, and rely upon this; therefore will this iniquity be to you like a falling breach, bent forwards in a high-towering wall, which falls to ruin suddenly, very suddenly. And He smites it to pieces, as a potter’s vessel falls to pieces, when they smash it without sparing, and of which, when it lies smashed to pieces there, you cannot find a sherd to fetch fire with from the hearth, or to take water with out of a cistern.”</hi> The “word” towards which they cherished <hi type="italic">me'ōs</hi> (read <hi type="italic">mo'oskhem</hi>), was the word of Jehovah through His prophet, which was directed against their untheocratic policy of reckoning upon Egypt. <hi type="italic">Nâlōz</hi>, bent out or twisted, is the term used to denote this very policy, which was ever resorting to bypaths and secret ways; whilst <hi type="italic">‛ōsheq</hi> denotes the squeezing out of the money required to carry on the war of freedom, and to purchase the help of Egypt (compare 2Ki 15:20). The guilt of Judah is compared to the broken and overhanging part of a high wall (<hi type="italic">nibh‛eh</hi>, bent forwards; compare (בּעבּע, a term applied to a diseased swelling). Just as such a broken piece brings down the whole of the injured wall along with it, so would the sinful conduct of Judah immediately ruin the whole of its existing constitution. Israel, which would not recognise itself as the image of Jehovah, even when there was yet time (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.16">Isa 29:16</reference>), would be like a vessel smashed into the smallest fragments. It is the captivity which is here figuratively threatened by the prophet; for the smashing had regard to Israel as a state. The subject to וּשׁברהּ in <reference osisRef="Isa.30.14">Isa 30:14</reference> is Jehovah, who would make use of the hostile power of man to destroy the wall, and break up the kingdom of Judah into such a diaspora of broken <hi type="italic">sherds</hi>. The reading is not ושׁהברהּ (lxx, Targum), but וּשׁברהּ, <hi type="italic">et franget eam</hi>. <hi type="italic">Kâthōth</hi> is an infinitive statement of the mode; the participle <hi type="italic">kâthūth</hi>, which is adopted by the Targum, Kimchi, Norzi, and others, is less suitable. It was necessary to proceed with יחמל לא (without his sparing), simply because the infinitive absolute cannot be connected with לא (Ewald, §350,<hi type="italic">a</hi>). לחשּׂוף (to be written thus with <hi type="italic">dagesh</hi> both here and Hag 2:16) passes from the primary meaning <hi type="italic">nudare</hi> to that of scooping up, as ערה does to that of pouring out.
entries.87920edfb6f902748ddf75c6c69790388bcce2c3: <reference osisRef="Isa.30.15-Isa.30.17">Isa 30:15-17</reference> <div eID="gen13191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13192" type="x-p"/> Into such small sherds, a heap thus scattered hither and thither, would the kingdom of Judah be broken up, in consequence of its ungodly thirst for self-liberation. <hi type="italic">“For thus saith the Lord Jehovah, the Holy One of Israel, Through turning and rest ye would be helped; your strength would show itself in quietness and confidence; but ye would not. And ye said, No, but we will fly upon horses; therefore ye shall flee: and, We will ride upon racehorses; therefore your pursuers will race. A thousand, ye will flee from the threatening of one, from the threatening of five, until ye are reduced to a remnant, like a pine upon the top of the mountain, and like a banner upon the hill.”</hi> The conditions upon which their salvation depended, and by complying with which they would attain to it, were <hi type="italic">shūbhâh</hi>, turning from their self-chosen way, and <hi type="italic">nachath</hi>, rest from self-confident work of their own (from <hi type="italic">nūăch</hi>, like <hi type="italic">rachath</hi>, <hi type="italic">ventilabrum</hi>, from <hi type="italic">rūăch</hi>, and <hi type="italic">shachath</hi>, <hi type="italic">fovea</hi>, from <hi type="italic">shūăch</hi>). Their strength (i.e., what they would be able to do in opposition to the imperial power) would show itself (<hi type="italic">hâyâh</hi>, arise, come to the light, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.29.2">Isa 29:2</reference>), in <hi type="italic">hashqēt</hi>, laying aside their busy care and stormy eagerness, and <hi type="italic">bitchâh</hi>, trust, which cleaves to Jehovah and, renouncing all self-help, leaves Him to act alone. This was the leading and fundamental principle of the prophet’s politics even in the time of Ahaz (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.4">Isa 7:4</reference>). But from the very first they would not act upon it; nor would they now that the alliance with Egypt had become an irreversible fact. To fly upon horses, and ride away upon racehorses (<hi type="italic">kal</hi>, like κέλης, <hi type="italic">celer</hi>)<note placement="foot">We regard the Sanscrit <hi type="italic">kal</hi>, to drive or hunt, the Greek κέλλ(ὀκέλλ)ειν, and the Semitic <hi type="italic">qal</hi>, as all having the same root: cf., Vurtius, <hi type="italic">Grundzüge der griech. Etymol</hi>. i. 116.)</note> had been and still was their proud and carnal ambition, which Jehovah would answer by fulfilling upon them the curses of the <hi type="italic">thorah</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.8">Lev 26:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.36">Lev 26:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.25">Deu 28:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.30">Deu 32:30</reference>).  One, or at the most five, of the enemy would be able with their snorting to put to flight a whole thousand of the men of Judah. The verb <hi type="italic">nūs</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.16">Isa 30:16</reference>), which rhymes with <hi type="italic">sūs</hi>, is used first of all in its primary sense of “flying” (related to <hi type="italic">nūts</hi>, cf., <reference osisRef="Exod.14.27">Exo 14:27</reference>), and then in its more usual sense of “fleeing.” (Luzzatto, after Abulwalîd: <hi type="italic">vogliamo far sui cavalli gloriosa comparsa</hi>, from <hi type="italic">nūs</hi>, or rather <hi type="italic">nâsas</hi>, hence <hi type="italic">nânōs</hi>, from which comes <hi type="italic">nēs</hi>, <hi type="italic">excellere</hi>.) יקּלּוּ, the fut. <hi type="italic">niphal</hi>, signifies to be light, i.e., swift; whereas יקל, the fut. <hi type="italic">kal</hi>, had become a common expression for light in the sense of despised or lightly esteemed. The horses and chariots are Judah’s own (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.7">Isa 2:7</reference>; Mic 5:9), though possibly with the additional allusion to the Egyptian cavalry, of world-wide renown, which they had called to their help. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.30.17">Isa 30:17</reference></hi> the subject of the first clause is also that of the second, and consequently we have not וּמפּני (compare the asyndeta in <reference osisRef="Isa.17.6">Isa 17:6</reference>). The insertion of <hi type="italic">rebhâbhâh</hi> (ten thousand) after <hi type="italic">chămisshâh</hi> (five), which Lowth, Gesenius, and others propose, is quite unnecessary. The play upon the words symbolizes the divine law of retribution (<hi type="italic">talio</hi>), which would be carried out with regard to them. The nation, which had hitherto resembled a thick forest, would become like a lofty pine (<hi type="italic">tōrne</hi>, according to the talmudic <hi type="italic">tūrnı̄thâ</hi>, <hi type="italic">Pinus pinea</hi>), standing solitary upon the top of a mountain, and like a flagstaff planted upon a hill - a miserable remnant in the broad land so fearfully devastated by war. For אם עד followed by a preterite (equivalent to the <hi type="italic">fut. exactum</hi>), compare <reference osisRef="Isa.6.11">Isa 6:11</reference> and Gen 24:19.
entries.61313013e9015ebf6a63f373635c22a596d92e18: <reference osisRef="Isa.30.18">Isa 30:18</reference> <div eID="gen13192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13193" type="x-p"/> The prophet now proceeds with ולכן, to which we cannot give any other meaning than <hi type="italic">et propterea</hi>, which it has everywhere else. The thought of the prophet is the perpetually recurring one, that Israel would have to be reduced to a small remnant before Jehovah would cease from His wrath. <hi type="italic">“And therefore will Jehovah wait till He inclines towards you, and therefore will He withdraw Himself on high till He has mercy upon you; for Jehovah is a God of right, salvation to those who wait for Him.”</hi> In other places <hi type="italic">lâkhēn</hi> (therefore) deduces the punishment from the sin; here it infers, from the nature of the punishment, the long continuance of the divine wrath. <hi type="italic">Chikkâh</hi>, to wait, connected as it is here with <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi>, has at least the idea, if not the actual signification, of <hi type="italic">delay</hi> (as in 2Ki 9:3; compare <reference osisRef="Job.32.4">Job 32:4</reference>). This helps to determine the sense of <hi type="italic">yârūm</hi>, which does not mean, He will show Himself exalted as a judge, that through judgment He may render it possible to have mercy upon you (which is too far-fetched a meaning); but, He will raise Himself up, so as to be far away (cf., Num 16:45, “Get you up from among this congregation;” and <reference osisRef="Ps.10.5">Psa 10:5</reference>, <hi type="italic">mârōm</hi> = “far above,” as far as heaven, out of his sight), that thus (after having for a long time withdrawn His gracious presence; cf., Hos 5:6) He may bestow His mercy upon you. A dark prospect, but only alarming to unbelievers. The salvation at the remotest end of the future belongs to believers even now. This is affirmed in the word <hi type="italic">'ashrē</hi> (blessed), which recalls Psa 2:12. The prophet uses <hi type="italic">châkhâh</hi> in a very significant double sense here, just as he did nuus a short time before. Jehovah is waiting for the time when He can show His favour once more, and blessed are they who meet His waiting with their own waiting.
entries.31ce4f57d7f6e07f7c1b2107b7f4c11c965ca5cb: <reference osisRef="Isa.30.19-Isa.30.22">Isa 30:19-22</reference> <div eID="gen13193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13194" type="x-p"/> None but such are heirs of the grace that follows the judgment - a people, newly pardoned in response to its cry for help, conducted by faithful teachers in the right way, and renouncing idolatry with disgust. <hi type="italic">“For a people continues dwelling in Zion, in Jerusalem; thou shalt not weep for ever: He will prove Himself gracious to thee at the sound of thy cry for help; as soon as He hears, He answers thee. And the Lord giveth you bread in penury, and water for your need; and thy teachers will not hide themselves any more, and thine eyes come to see thy teachers. And thine ears will hear words behind thee, saying, 'This is the way, walk ye in it!' whether ye turn to the right hand or to the left. And ye defile the covering of thy graven images of silver, and the clothing of thy molten images of gold; thou wilt scatter them like filthy thing: 'Get out!' thou sayest to it.”</hi> We do not render <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.30.19">Isa 30:19</reference></hi>, “For O people that dwelleth in Zion, in Jerusalem!” For although the personal pronoun may be omitted after <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> in an apostrophizing connection (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.5">Pro 8:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.23">Joe 2:23</reference>), we should certainly expect to find אתּה here. The accent very properly marks these words as forming an independent clause. The apparent tautology in the expression, “in Zion, in Jerusalem,” is emphatic and explanatory. The fate of Zion-Jerusalem will not be the same as that of the imperial city (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.20">Isa 13:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.25.2">Isa 25:2</reference>); for it is the city of Jehovah, which, according to His promise, cannot become an eternally deserted ruin. After this promising declaration, the prophet turns and addresses the people of the future in the people of his own time; <hi type="italic">bâkhō</hi> strengthens the verbal notion with the mark of duration; <hi type="italic">chânōn</hi> with the mark of certainty and fulness. יחנך, with an advanced <hi type="italic">ŏ</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.43.29">Gen 43:29</reference>, for יחן. כּ is the shortest expression used to denote simultaneous occurrence; answering and hearing would coincide (<hi type="italic">shom‛âh</hi>, <hi type="italic">nomen actionis</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.47.9">Isa 47:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.55.2">Isa 55:2</reference>; Ges. §45, 1 <hi type="italic">b</hi>; <hi type="italic">‛ânâkh</hi>, the pausal form here, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.23.37">Jer 23:37</reference>). From this lowest stage of response to the penitential cry for help, the promise rises higher and higher. The next stage is that in which Jerusalem is brought into all the distress consequent upon a siege, as threatened by the prophet in <reference osisRef="Isa.29.3-Isa.29.4">Isa 29:3-4</reference>; the besieged would not be allowed by God to die of starvation, but He would send them the necessary support. The same expression, but very little altered, viz., “to give to eat <hi type="italic">lechem lachatz ūmayim lachatz</hi>,” signifies to put any one upon the low rations of a siege or of imprisonment, in 1Ki 22:27 and <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.26">2Ch 18:26</reference>; but here it is a promise, with the threat kept in the background. צר and לחץ are connected with the absolute nouns לחם and מים, not as adverbial, but as appositional definitions (like תּרעלה יין, “wine which is giddiness,” in <reference osisRef="Ps.60.5">Psa 60:5</reference>; and בּרכּים מים, “water which is knees,” i.e., which has the measure of the knees, where <hi type="italic">birkayim</hi> is also in apposition, and not the accusative of measurement): literally, bread which is necessity, and water which is affliction; that is to say, nourishment of which there is extreme need, the very opposite of bread and water in abundance. Umbreit and Drechsler understand this spiritually. But the promise rises as it goes on. There is already an advance, in the fact that the faithful and well-meaning teachers (<hi type="italic">mōrı̄m</hi>) no longer keep themselves hidden because of the hard-heartedness and hatred of the people, as they have done ever since the time of Ahaz (נכנף, a denom.: to withdraw into כּנף, πτέρυξ, the utmost end, the most secret corner; though <hi type="italic">kânaph</hi> in itself signifies to cover or conceal). Israel, when penitent, would once more be able to rejoice in the sight of those whom it longed to have back again. מוריך is a plural, according to the context (on the singular of the previous predicate, see Ges. §147). As the shepherds of the flock, they would follow the people with friendly words of admonition, whilst the people would have their ears open to receive their instruction. תּאמינוּ is here equivalent to תּימינוּ, תּימינוּ. The abominations of idolatry (which continued even in the first years of Hezekiah’s reign: <reference osisRef="Isa.31.7">Isa 31:7</reference>; Mic 1:5; Mic 5:11-13; Mic 6:16) would now be regarded as abominations, and put away. Even gold and silver, with which the images that were either carved or cast in inferior metal were overlaid, would be made unclean (see 2 Kings 28:8ff.); that is to say, no use would be made of them. <hi type="italic">Dâvâh</hi> is a shorter expression for <hi type="italic">kelı̄</hi> <hi type="italic">dâvâh</hi>, the cloth worn by a woman at the monthly period. On <hi type="italic">zârâh</hi>, to dispense - to which <hi type="italic">dâvâh</hi> would be inappropriate if understood of the woman herself, as it is by Luzzatto - compare 2Ki 23:6. With זהבך, the plural used in the general address passes over into the individualizing singular; לו is to be taken as a neuter pointing back to the plunder of idols.
entries.7dff62bb969589b351a5540dd02a608f58d7fd62: <reference osisRef="Isa.30.23-Isa.30.25">Isa 30:23-25</reference> <div eID="gen13194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13195" type="x-p"/> The promise, after setting forth this act of penitence, rises higher and higher; it would not stop at bread in time of need. <hi type="italic">“And He gives rain to thy seed, with which thou sowest the land; and bread of the produce of the land, and it is full of sap and fat: in that day your flocks will feed in roomy pastures. And the oxen and the young asses, which work the land, salted mash will they eat, which is winnowed with the winnowing shovel and winnowing fork! And upon every high mountain, and every hill that rises high, there are springs, brooks in the day of the great massacre, when the towers fall.”</hi> The blessing which the prophet depicts is the reverse of the day of judgment, and stands in the foreground when the judgment is past. The expression “in that day” fixes, as it were, the evening of the day of judgment, which is followed by the depicted morning of blessing. But the great mass of the Jewish nation would be first of all murdered in war; the towers must fall, i.e., (though without any figure, and merely as an exemplifying expression) all the bulwarks of self-confidence, self-help, and pride (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.15">Isa 2:15</reference>; Mic 5:9-10). In the place of the self-induced calamities of war, there would now come the God-given rich blessings of peace; and in the place of the proud towers, there would come fruitful heights abounding with water. The field would be cultivated again, and produce luxuriant crops of nutritious corn; so that not only the labour of man, but that of the animals also, would receive a rich reward. “Rain to thy seed:” this is the early rain commencing about the middle of October. אשׁר as an accusative, זרע being construed with a double accusative, as in Deu 22:9. מקניך might be the singular, so far as the form is concerned (see <reference osisRef="Isa.1.30">Isa 1:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.12">Isa 5:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.11">Isa 22:11</reference>); but, according to <reference osisRef="Exod.17.3">Exo 17:3</reference>, it must be taken as a plural, like מוריך. The <hi type="italic">'ălâphı̄m</hi> are the oxen used in ploughing and threshing; the <hi type="italic">‛ăyârı̄m</hi>, the asses used for carrying manure, soil, the sheaves, or the grain. <hi type="italic">Belı̄l</hi> <hi type="italic">châmı̄ts</hi> is a mash (composed of oats, barley, and vetches, or things of that kind) made more savoury with salt and sour vegetables;<note placement="foot">Such as <hi type="italic">Salsola kali</hi>, <hi type="italic">Salsola tragus</hi>, <hi type="italic">Salsola soda</hi>, and other plants of the family of the <hi type="italic">chenopodiaceae</hi>.</note> that is to say, a <hi type="italic">farrago</hi> (from <hi type="italic">bâlal</hi>, to mix; <hi type="italic">Comm. on Job</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Job.40.19-Job.40.24">Job 40:19-24</reference>). According to Wetzstein, it is ripe barley (unthreshed during the harvest and threshing time, and the grain itself for the rest of the year) mixed with salt or salt vegetables. In any case, <hi type="italic">belı̄l</hi> is to be understood as referring to the grain; this is evident from the relative clause, “which has been winnowed” (= <hi type="italic">mezōreh</hi>, Ewald, §169,<hi type="italic">d</hi>), or perhaps more correctly, “which he (one) winnows” (<hi type="italic">part. kal</hi>), the participle standing for the third person, with the subject contained within itself (Ewald, §200), i.e., not what was generally given from economy, viz., barley, etc., mixed with chopped straw (<hi type="italic">tibn</hi>), but pure grain (<hi type="italic">habb</hi> <hi type="italic">mahd</hi>, as they say at the present day). <hi type="italic">Rachath</hi> is a winnowing shovel, which is still used, according to Wetzstein, in <hi type="italic">Merj. Gedur</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Hauran</hi>; <hi type="italic">mizreh</hi>, on the other hand, is the winnowing fork with six prongs. Dainty food, such as was only given occasionally to the cattle, as something especially strengthening, would then be their regular food, and would be prepared in the most careful manner. “Who cannot see,” exclaims Vitringa, “that this is to be taken spiritually?” He appeals to what Paul says in <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.9">1Co 9:9</reference>, viz., that God does not trouble Himself about oxen. But Paul did not mean this in the same sense as Aristotle, who maintained that the <hi type="italic">minima</hi> were entirely excluded from the providence of God. What the Scriptures say concerning cattle, they do not say for the sake of the cattle, but for the sake of men; though it does not follow that the cattle are to be understood figuratively, as representing men. And this is the case here. What the prophet paints in this idyllic style, in colours furnished by the existing customs,<note placement="foot">Asses particularly, even those of a guest, are generally very much neglected. The host throws them a little grass, and then hangs up the fodder-sack full of chopped straw; and it is a sign of extraordinary hospitality of corn is given to the asses as well as to the horses. - Wetzstein.</note> is not indeed intended to be understood in the letter; and yet it is to be taken literally. In the age of glory, even on this side of eternity, a gigantic stride will be taken forward towards the glorification of universal nature, and towards the end of all those sighs which are so discernible now, more especially among domestic animals. The prophecy is therefore to be interpreted according to Rom 8:19.; from which we may clearly see that God does trouble Himself about the sighing of an ox or ass that is overburdened with severe toil, and sometimes left to starve.
entries.e062db0eb08df437d0bd6a15885b3ff2107df212: <reference osisRef="Isa.30.26">Isa 30:26</reference> <div eID="gen13195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13196" type="x-p"/> The promise now rises higher and higher, and passes from earth to heaven. <hi type="italic">“And the light of the moon will be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be multiplied sevenfold, like the light of seven days, in the day that Jehovah bindeth the hurt of His people, and healeth the crushing of His stroke.”</hi> Modern commentators from Lowth downwards for the most part pronounce היּמים שׁבעת כּאור a gloss; and there is one external evidence in favour of this, which is wanting in the case of the other supposed glosses in Isaiah, namely, that the words are omitted by the lxx (though not by the Targum, the Syriac, or Jerome). Even Luther (although he notices these words in his exposition and sermons) merely renders them, <hi type="italic">der Sonnen schein wird siebenmal heller sein denn jtzt</hi> (the sunlight will be seven times as bright as it is now). But the internal evidence does not favour their spuriousness even in the case before us; for the fact that the regularity of the verse, as consisting of four members, is thereby disturbed, is no evidence at all, since the v. could be warranted in a pentastic quite as well as in a tetrastic form. We therefore decide in this instance also in favour of the conclusion that the prophet composed the gloss himself. But we cannot maintain, with Umbreit, that the addition was necessary, in order to guard against the idea that there would be seven suns shining in the sky; for the prophet does not predict a multiplication of the sun by seven, but simply the multiplication of its light. The seven days are the length of an ordinary week. Drechsler gives it correctly: “The radiated light, which is sufficient to produce the daylight for a whole week according to the existing order of things, will then be concentrated into a single day.” Luther renders it in this way, <hi type="italic">als wenn sieben tag ynn eynander geschlossen weren</hi> (as if seven days were enclosed in one another). This also is not meant figuratively, any more than Paul means is figuratively, when he says, that with the manifestation of the “glory” of the children of God, the “corruption” of universal nature will come to an end. Nevertheless, it is not of the new heaven that the prophet is speaking, but of the glorification of nature, which is promised by both the Old Testament prophecy and by that of the New at the closing period of the world’s history, and which will be the closing typical self-annunciation of that eternal glory in which everything will be swallowed up. The brightest, sunniest days then alternate, as the prophet foretells, with the most brilliant moonlight nights. No other miracles will be needed for this than that wonder-working power of God, which even now produces those changes of weather, the laws of which no researches of natural science have enabled us to calculate, and which will then give the greatest brilliancy and most unchangeable duration to what is now comparatively rare - namely, a perfectly unclouded sky, with sun or moon shining in all its brilliancy, yet without any scorching from the one, or injurious effects from the other. Heaven and earth will then put on their sabbath dress; for it will be the Sabbath of the world’s history, the seventh day in the world’s week. The light of the seven days of the world’s week will be all concentrated in the seventh. For the beginning of creation was light, and its close will be light as well. The darkness all comes between, simply that it may be overcome. At last will come a <hi type="italic">bōqer</hi> (morning), after which it will no more be said, “And evening was, and morning was.” The prophet is speaking of the last type of this morning. What he predicts here precedes what he predicted in <reference osisRef="Isa.24.23">Isa 24:23</reference>, just as the date of its composition precedes that of chapters 24-27; for there the imperial city was Babylon, whereas here the glory of the latter day is still placed immediately after the fall of Assyria.
entries.0bc52c623d6b10ff996a02f17863b52b6675d1a7: <reference osisRef="Isa.30.27-Isa.30.28">Isa 30:27-28</reference> <hi type="italic">“Behold, the name of Jehovah cometh from far, burning His wrath, and quantity of smoke: His lips are full of wrathful foam, and His tongue like devouring fire. And His breath is like an overflowing brook, which reaches half-way to the neck, to sift nations in the sieve of nothingness; and a misleading bridle comes to the cheeks of the nations.”</hi> Two figures are here melted together - namely, that of a storm coming up from the farthest horizon, which turns the sky into a sea of fire, and kindles whatever it strikes, so that there rises up a heavy burden, or thick mass of smoke (<hi type="italic">kōbhed massâ'âh</hi>, like <hi type="italic">mas'ēth</hi> in Jdg 20:40, cf., Jdg 20:38; on this attributive combination, burning His wrath (Ewald, §288,<hi type="italic">c</hi>) and a quantity, etc., see <reference osisRef="Isa.13.9">Isa 13:9</reference>); and that of a man burning with wrath, whose lips foam, whose tongue moves to and fro like a flame, and whose breath is a snorting that threatens destruction, which when it issues from Jehovah swells into a stream, which so far covers a man that only his neck appears as the visible half. We had the same figure in <reference osisRef="Isa.8.8">Isa 8:8</reference>, where Asshur, as it came upon Judah, was compared to such an almost overwhelming and drowning flood. Here, again, it refers to Judah, which the wrath of Jehovah had almost though not entirely destroyed. For the ultimate object of the advancing name of Jehovah (<hi type="italic">shēm</hi>, name, relating to His judicial coming) is to sift nations, etc.: <hi type="italic">lahănâphâh</hi> for <hi type="italic">lehânı̄ph</hi> (like <hi type="italic">lahăzâdâh</hi> in <reference osisRef="Dan.5.20">Dan 5:20</reference>), to make it more like <hi type="italic">nâphâh</hi> in sound. The <hi type="italic">sieve of nothingness</hi> is a sieve in which everything, that does not remain in it as good corn, is given up to annihilation; שׁוא is want of being, i.e., of life from God, and denotes the fate that properly belongs to such worthlessness. In the case of <hi type="italic">v'resen</hi> (and a bridle, etc.) we must either supply in thought לשׂום (שׂם), or, what is better, take it as a substantive clause: “a misleading bridle” (or a bridle of misleading, as Böttcher renders it, <hi type="italic">math‛eh</hi> being the form <hi type="italic">mashqeh</hi>) holds the cheeks of the nations. The nations are regarded as wild horses, which could not be tamed, but which were now so firmly bound and controlled by the wrath of God, that they were driven down into the abyss.
entries.fa2cf343f7a6577bf5ac0145d4d3228ba30492e7: <reference osisRef="Isa.30.29">Isa 30:29</reference> <div eID="gen13196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13197" type="x-p"/> This is the issue of the judgment which begins at the house of God, then turns against the instrument employed, namely the heathen, and becomes to the Israel that survives a counterpart of the deliverance from Egypt. <hi type="italic">“Your song will then sound as in the night, when the feast is celebrated; and ye will have joy of heart like those who march with the playing of flutes, to go up to the mountain of Jehovah, to the Rock of Israel.”</hi> In the word <hi type="italic">châg</hi> (feast), which is generally used with special reference to the feast of tabernacles, there is here an unmistakeable allusion to the passover, as we may see from the introduction of “the night,” which evidently means the night before the passover (<hi type="italic">lēl shimmurı̄m</hi>, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.42">Exo 12:42</reference>), which was so far a festal night, that it preceded and introduced the feast of unleavened bread. The prophet has taken his figure from the first passover-night in Egypt, when Israel was rejoicing in the deliverance which it was just about to receive, whilst the destroying angel was passing through the land. Such would be the song which they would be able to sing, when Jehovah poured out His judgment upon His people’s enemies outside. The church is shut up in its chamber (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.20">Isa 26:20</reference>), and its joy resembles the heartfelt joy of those who go on pilgrimage on one of the three great feasts, or in the procession that carries up the first-fruits to Jerusalem (<hi type="italic">Biccurim</hi>, iii. 3), going up with the sound of flutes to the mountain of Jehovah, to appear before Him, the Rock of Israel.
entries.5781b774da9df16418e95d15a079d278f17fe1b2: <reference osisRef="Isa.30.30-Isa.30.33">Isa 30:30-33</reference> <div eID="gen13197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13198" type="x-p"/> Israel is marching in such a joyful way to a sacred and glorious height, whilst outside Jehovah is sweeping the world-power entirely away, and that without any help from Israel. <hi type="italic">“And Jehovah causes His majestic voice to be heard, and causes the lowering of His arm to be seen, with the snorting of wrath and the blazing of devouring fire, the bursting of a cloud, and pouring of rain and hailstones. For Asshur will be terrified at the voice of Jehovah, when He smites with the staff. And it will come to pass, every stroke of the rod of destiny, which Jehovah causes to fall upon Asshur, is dealt amidst the noise of drums and the playing of guitars; and in battles of swinging arm He fights it. For a place for the sacrifice of abominations has long been made ready, even for the king is it prepared; deep, broad has He made it: its funeral-pile has fire and wood in abundance; the breath of Jehovah like a stream of brimstone sets it on fire.”</hi> The imposing crash (on <hi type="italic">hōd</hi>, see <reference osisRef="Job.39.20">Job 39:20</reference>) of the cry which Jehovah causes to be heard is thunder (see <reference osisRef="Ps.29.1-Ps.29.11">Psa 29:1-11</reference>); for the catastrophe occurs with a discharge of all the destructive forces of a storm (see <reference osisRef="Isa.29.6">Isa 29:6</reference>). <hi type="italic">Nephets</hi> is the “breaking up” or “bursting,” viz., of a cloud. It is through such wrath-announcing phenomena of nature that Jehovah manifests the otherwise invisible letting down of His arm to smite (<hi type="italic">nachath</hi> may possibly not be the derivative of <hi type="italic">nūăch</hi>, “settling down,” but of <hi type="italic">nâchath</hi>, “the coming down,” as in <reference osisRef="Ps.38.3">Psa 38:3</reference>; just as <hi type="italic">shebheth</hi> in <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.7">2Sa 23:7</reference> is not derived from <hi type="italic">shūbh</hi>, but from <hi type="italic">shâbhath</hi>, to go to ruin). <reference osisRef="Isa.30.31">Isa 30:31</reference>, commencing with <hi type="italic">ki</hi> (for), explains the terrible nature of what occurs, from the object at which it is directed: Asshur is alarmed at the voice of Jehovah, and thoroughly goes to pieces. We must not render this, as the Targum does, “which smites with the rod,” i.e., which bears itself so haughtily, so tyrannically (after <reference osisRef="Isa.10.24">Isa 10:24</reference>). The smiter here is Jehovah (lxx, Vulg., Luther); and <hi type="italic">basshēbhet</hi> <hi type="italic">yakkeh</hi> is either an attributive clause, or, better still, a circumstantial determining clause, <hi type="italic">eo virga percutiente</hi>.
